stimulus: Town councilor: At last week's public hearing, not one resident presented any evidence that the new downtown parking meters have driven shoppers away. Since no such evidence has been offered, the meters clearly have not hurt downtown retail business, and the council should keep them in place.
stem: The councilor's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: takes the absence of presented evidence that the meters hurt business as proof that they have not
choices.B: ignores the possibility that the meters generate revenue the town could use to support downtown retail businesses
choices.C: assumes that the meters are the only factor that could possibly have affected the level of downtown retail business
choices.D: attacks the character of residents who want the meters removed instead of answering their arguments on the merits
choices.E: generalizes from the residents who attended one hearing to the views of all of the shoppers who visit downtown

explanations.A: Correct. The only premise is that no evidence of harm was offered, which does not show that there is no harm; absence of proof is treated as proof of absence.
explanations.B: Out of scope: meter revenue is never mentioned, and the conclusion is about harm to business, not about alternative uses of money.
explanations.C: Extreme: the councilor never claims the meters are the only factor; the argument fails even if other factors exist.
explanations.D: Wrong part: the councilor attacks no one's character; the residents are said only to have offered no evidence.
explanations.E: Wrong part: the argument is about what evidence was presented, not about what the attendees' opinions say about all shoppers.

keyTakeaway: A lack of evidence for a claim does not establish that the claim is false.
predictionHint: No evidence of harm offered, therefore no harm: lack of support treated as falsity.

stimulus: Historian: The monks of Saint Orrin's abbey wrote that the famine of 1340 was the worst in the region's history. But the abbey stood in the very district that suffered most, and chroniclers tend to exaggerate the importance of events they lived through. We must therefore conclude that the abbey's account of the famine is worthless as evidence.
stem: The historian's argument is flawed in that it

choices.A: fails to establish that the famine of 1340 was in fact the worst that the region has ever experienced
choices.B: infers that the account is wholly unreliable from a tendency that would at most make it exaggerated
choices.C: relies on a source whose authors had no means of learning how severe the famine was in other parts of the region
choices.D: assumes that the monks were the only people in the region who made a written record of the famine
choices.E: presumes that the abbey stood in the district where the largest number of monks in the region lived

explanations.A: Wrong part: the historian never asserts that the famine was the worst; the claim in question is that the account is worthless.
explanations.B: Correct. A tendency to exaggerate would lower the account's reliability, not eliminate it; the account could still be good evidence that a severe famine occurred. The conclusion 'worthless' goes far beyond the premise.
explanations.C: Out of scope: what the monks could know about other regions is not what the historian cites against them.
explanations.D: Extreme: the argument does not depend on the monks being the only recorders.
explanations.E: Out of scope: where most monks lived plays no role in the reasoning.

keyTakeaway: Evidence of possible bias supports discounting a source, not discarding it entirely.
predictionHint: Possible exaggeration does not make the whole account worthless.

stimulus: Orchard manager: Without honeybees, an apple orchard cannot be well pollinated. Our orchard keeps forty hives on its grounds this year. Therefore, our apple blossoms will be well pollinated this spring.
stem: The reasoning in the manager's argument is flawed because it

choices.A: assumes that honeybees are the only insects that pollinate apple blossoms in orchards of this kind
choices.B: overlooks that the hives might be moved off the grounds before the blossoms have opened this spring
choices.C: treats a condition that is required for good pollination as if it were enough to ensure it
choices.D: draws a conclusion about one particular orchard from a premise about apple orchards in general terms
choices.E: takes for granted that well-pollinated blossoms will go on to produce a large and profitable harvest

explanations.A: Extreme: the first premise says bees are necessary, which is the opposite of saying they are the only pollinators that matter.
explanations.B: Out of scope: the manager says the hives are kept on the grounds; the flaw would remain even if they stay there.
explanations.C: Correct. 'Without bees, no good pollination' makes bees necessary. The conclusion treats the presence of bees as sufficient, ignoring weather, bloom timing and other requirements.
explanations.D: Wrong part: applying a general premise to a particular case is ordinarily valid and is not the error here.
explanations.E: Out of scope: the conclusion concerns pollination, not harvest size.

keyTakeaway: If X is required for Y, having X does not guarantee Y.
predictionHint: Necessary condition mistaken for a sufficient one.

stimulus: Budget analyst: Of the eleven county departments whose budgets were increased last year, nine have since recorded faster service-response times. Of the six departments whose budgets were cut, only one has recorded faster response times. Clearly, raising a department's budget is the best way to speed up its service.
stem: The analyst's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: overlooks that departments with smaller budgets may serve far fewer residents than the larger departments do
choices.B: compares the number of departments that improved in each group instead of the proportion of each group that improved
choices.C: assumes that every department that sped up its service had previously received a budget increase
choices.D: bases a claim that one method is best on a comparison with only one alternative, cutting funds
choices.E: presumes that faster response times are the only measure by which a department's service quality can be judged

explanations.A: Out of scope: the number of residents served is not something the conclusion or data turn on.
explanations.B: Wrong part: the analyst does compare proportions (nine of eleven against one of six), and those proportions favor the claim.
explanations.C: Reversal: the data say nothing about all departments that sped up, and the argument does not need that claim.
explanations.D: Correct. The data contrast budget increases only with budget cuts. 'Best way' requires comparison with other methods such as reorganization or staffing changes, which are never considered.
explanations.E: True but irrelevant: the conclusion is explicitly about speed of response, not overall service quality.

keyTakeaway: A claim that something is the best way needs comparison with more than one alternative; beating the worst option proves little.
predictionHint: Increase beats cut, but 'best way' needs other methods compared.

stimulus: Extension agent: Most of the orchards in the valley that adopted drip irrigation last decade have recorded higher yields. Furthermore, most of the orchards that recorded higher yields also replanted with new rootstock. So most of the valley's orchards that adopted drip irrigation also replanted with new rootstock.
stem: The reasoning in the agent's argument is flawed in that it

choices.A: treats a correlation between drip irrigation and higher yields as evidence of a causal connection between the two
choices.B: fails to specify what proportion of the orchards is meant by 'most' in each of the statements it makes
choices.C: overlooks that some orchards may have replanted with new rootstock before they adopted drip irrigation at all
choices.D: assumes that the orchards that adopted drip irrigation are representative of all of the orchards in the valley
choices.E: infers that most of one group are in a third group because most are in a second group and most of that group are in the third

explanations.A: Wrong part: the agent draws no causal conclusion; the conclusion is a claim about overlap between groups.
explanations.B: True but irrelevant: precisifying 'most' would not repair the structural gap.
explanations.C: Out of scope: the order of events does not matter to a claim about overlap.
explanations.D: Wrong part: the conclusion concerns orchards that adopted irrigation; no generalization to all orchards is made.
explanations.E: Correct. 'Most D are H' and 'most H are R' do not give 'most D are R': the H orchards that replanted may come largely from outside D. Majorities do not chain.

keyTakeaway: 'Most A are B' and 'most B are C' never guarantee 'most A are C.'
predictionHint: Most-most chain: the overlap may be located entirely outside the first group.

stimulus: Most of the grain elevators in Dunmore County were built before 1950. Every elevator in the county built before 1950 lacks a modern fire-suppression system. Several elevators built since then have had such systems installed.
stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.A: Most of the grain elevators in Dunmore County lack a modern fire-suppression system.
choices.B: Every elevator in the county that lacks a modern fire-suppression system was built before the year 1950.
choices.C: Every elevator in the county built since 1950 has been equipped with a modern fire-suppression system.
choices.D: Elevators built before 1950 in Dunmore County are more likely to catch fire than newer elevators are.
choices.E: Nearly all of the grain elevators in Dunmore County lack a modern fire-suppression system.

explanations.A: Correct. More than half the elevators are pre-1950, and every one of those lacks a system, so more than half lack one.
explanations.B: Reversal: the facts say all pre-1950 elevators lack systems, not that only pre-1950 elevators lack them.
explanations.C: Necessary v sufficient: some newer elevators have had systems installed, but nothing says every newer one has.
explanations.D: Out of scope: fire likelihood is never discussed.
explanations.E: Extreme: 'most' is supported, but 'nearly all' would require the pre-1950 share to be very large.

keyTakeaway: On most-strongly-supported questions, choose the claim that goes no further than the force of the statements.
predictionHint: A majority are old, all old ones lack systems, so a majority lack them.

stimulus: Archivist: The Brandt collection of census schedules contains many handwritten schedules. No handwritten schedule in the collection has been digitized. Nevertheless, a number of the schedules in the collection have been digitized, and these are now searchable online by name.
stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.A: Most of the schedules in the collection are not handwritten.
choices.B: Some of the schedules in the collection are not handwritten.
choices.C: Every schedule in the collection that has not been digitized is handwritten.
choices.D: Digitizing handwritten schedules is not practical for the collection's archivists.
choices.E: Fewer than half of the schedules in the collection are searchable online by name.

explanations.A: Wrong force: the digitized schedules prove only that some are not handwritten; 'most' is unsupported.
explanations.B: Correct. Digitized schedules exist and none of them is handwritten, so at least some schedules are not handwritten.
explanations.C: Reversal: the facts exclude handwritten schedules from digitization, not non-digitized schedules from being typed or printed.
explanations.D: Out of scope: the reasons digitization has not occurred are never given.
explanations.E: Extreme: nothing gives the proportion of digitized schedules, so no comparison with half is supported.

keyTakeaway: A 'no X is Y' statement plus the existence of some Y proves that some Y are not X.
predictionHint: Digitized ones exist; none is handwritten; so some schedules are not handwritten.

stimulus: Planning commission report: From 2015 to 2025, the number of building permits issued annually in Carver County rose by 40 percent, while the number of permit inspectors on the county's staff stayed the same. Every permit issued in the county must be approved by one of those inspectors. Over the same period, the average time between a permit application and its approval grew from 12 days to 31 days.
stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.A: The growth in the time needed to approve a permit was caused by the failure to hire more permit inspectors.
choices.B: The county should have hired more permit inspectors at some point between 2015 and 2025.
choices.C: The average number of permits approved annually per inspector was greater in 2025 than in 2015.
choices.D: The number of permit applications submitted annually rose by more than 40 percent between 2015 and 2025.
choices.E: Every permit inspector in the county took longer to approve a typical application in 2025 than in 2015.

explanations.A: Wrong force: the report notes a coincidence of timing but does not say the staffing level caused the delay.
explanations.B: Out of scope: this is a recommendation, and the report states no goals or costs.
explanations.C: Correct. Issued permits rose 40 percent, all were approved by the same number of inspectors, so each inspector approved more permits on average.
explanations.D: Half right: applications and issued permits are different counts, and the approval rate could have risen or fallen; the report does not say.
explanations.E: Extreme: the report gives only an overall average time, not the experience of each inspector.

keyTakeaway: Do the arithmetic the stimulus allows, and refuse causal or prescriptive leaps it does not.
predictionHint: More permits, same inspectors: more permits per inspector.

stimulus: Council member: The Riverton public library should stay open until nine o'clock on weekday evenings. In a recent survey, a majority of residents said they would use the library more if it were open later. Extending the hours will therefore increase total use of the library.
stem: The council member's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.A: Extending evening hours would not require the library to shorten its weekend hours or reduce its other services.
choices.B: Most Riverton residents who responded to the survey do not currently use the library at all.
choices.C: No other improvement to the library would increase its use by more than later evening hours would.
choices.D: Residents who say they would use the library more if it were open later would actually do so.
choices.E: The value of a public library is best measured by the amount of use that it receives from residents.

explanations.A: Out of scope: the conclusion is about total use, and shortening weekend hours is a side issue the argument does not address.
explanations.B: Out of scope: even regular users could use the library more, so non-use is not required.
explanations.C: Comparison shift: the argument does not claim that later hours are the best way to raise use, only that they would raise it.
explanations.D: Correct. The argument moves from what residents say they would do to what they would do. If stated intentions did not translate into behavior, the conclusion would fail.
explanations.E: Wrong part: the conclusion is about use, not about how a library's value is measured.

keyTakeaway: When an argument moves from what people say to what they do, the assumption is that the statement predicts the behavior.
predictionHint: Survey answers (intentions) must reflect actual future behavior.

stimulus: Economist: A town's weekly farmers' market raises downtown shop revenue only if market shoppers also spend money in downtown shops. A survey of two hundred shoppers leaving Greer's market on a recent Saturday found that none had visited, or planned to visit, a downtown shop that day. Thus Greer's market does not raise downtown shop revenue.
stem: The economist's argument requires assuming which one of the following?

choices.A: The survey of the market shoppers was carried out by researchers who had no stake in the success of the market.
choices.B: Shoppers generally prefer to buy their goods at a farmers' market rather than at an ordinary shop.
choices.C: In other towns, shoppers at weekly farmers' markets do not spend money in the downtown shops there.
choices.D: Downtown shops that sell goods similar to those sold at the market lose some of their business to it.
choices.E: The shoppers surveyed were typical of Greer's market shoppers in how often they spend money downtown.

explanations.A: Wrong part: researcher neutrality is a different concern; the argument needs only that the sample reflects the shoppers.
explanations.B: Out of scope: shoppers' preferences are not part of the reasoning about whether downtown revenue rises.
explanations.C: Comparison shift: the conclusion concerns Greer only, so what happens in other towns is not required.
explanations.D: Out of scope: losing business to the market would be a different effect and the argument needs no claim about it.
explanations.E: Correct. The survey covered one Saturday's departing shoppers. If they differed from Greer's market shoppers generally, the finding would not support the claim about the market's effect on revenue.

keyTakeaway: A conclusion drawn from a survey needs the sample to be representative of the population it is about.
predictionHint: The surveyed Saturday shoppers must be typical of all market shoppers.

stimulus: Dairy owner: Switching my herd to robotic milking will make my farm more profitable. Robotic milking requires far fewer hired workers, so it will lower my labor costs substantially.
stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the dairy owner's argument?

choices.A: The savings in labor costs will not be outweighed by other costs of adopting robotic milking.
choices.B: Robotic milking will increase the amount of milk that each cow in the herd produces.
choices.C: Most dairy farms that have adopted robotic milking have become more profitable as a result.
choices.D: Labor is the largest single expense that a dairy farm has to meet.
choices.E: No change other than robotic milking could lower the farm's labor costs by a comparable amount.

explanations.A: Correct. The owner moves from lower labor costs to higher profit; if equipment, maintenance and energy costs ate up the savings, profit would not rise.
explanations.B: Out of scope: output per cow is not mentioned and profit could rise through savings alone.
explanations.C: Wrong force: this would support the claim, but the argument does not require that other farms have profited.
explanations.D: Extreme: labor need not be the largest expense for its reduction to matter.
explanations.E: Extreme: other ways of cutting labor costs might exist without undermining the claim that this one will help.

keyTakeaway: When one factor in a profit calculation changes, the argument assumes the other factors do not cancel it.
predictionHint: Lower labor costs only raise profit if new costs do not offset them.

stimulus: Historian: The surviving Thornby charter, dated 1182, must be a forgery. Its text calls the town a 'borough,' a word that did not come into common legal use until about a century after 1182, so no clerk of that year could have written it.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the historian's argument?

choices.A: Forged charters were common in the region during the twelfth century, particularly in prosperous towns.
choices.B: The surviving charter is a copy made a century later by a scribe who updated the original's terms.
choices.C: The charter was kept for most of its history in a secure town archive guarded by municipal officers.
choices.D: Other charters issued in 1182 describe their towns using the older word 'burgh' rather than 'borough.'
choices.E: Some historians have long maintained that the Thornby charter is a genuine document from its stated year.

explanations.A: Opposite: common forgery would make a forgery more likely, so this strengthens the argument.
explanations.B: Correct. If the surviving text is a later copy with modernized wording, the late word is explained without any forgery.
explanations.C: True but irrelevant: secure storage does not bear on whether the wording could date from 1182.
explanations.D: Opposite: it supports the claim that clerks in 1182 used a different word, strengthening the argument.
explanations.E: Wrong force: what historians have maintained is a matter of opinion and offers no reason about the word.

keyTakeaway: To weaken an inference from a single telltale feature, supply an innocent explanation of that feature.
predictionHint: Offer another way the anachronistic word could have entered the text.

stimulus: Agronomists compared soybean fields in the Marrow Basin and found that fields treated with Agrosan fungicide yielded about 12 percent more soybeans than untreated fields. The agronomists concluded that applying Agrosan raises soybean yields.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously calls into question the agronomists' conclusion?

choices.A: Agrosan costs more per acre than most of the other fungicides that are used on soybean crops.
choices.B: Some untreated fields also produced above-average soybean yields.
choices.C: The farmers who chose to apply Agrosan were mostly those who also planted higher-yielding seed varieties.
choices.D: The size of the yield increase on treated fields varied considerably from one field to another.
choices.E: Fungicides similar to Agrosan have raised yields of other crops grown in the region in several earlier studies.

explanations.A: Out of scope: the price of the fungicide does not bear on whether it raises yields.
explanations.B: Half right: a few high-yield untreated fields leave the average difference unexplained, so the argument is hardly affected.
explanations.C: Correct. If treated fields were already planted with better seed, the seed could account for the whole difference, which undermines the causal conclusion.
explanations.D: True but irrelevant: variation in the size of the effect is compatible with a real average effect.
explanations.E: Opposite: success with similar products in other crops supports the conclusion.

keyTakeaway: To weaken a causal claim from a comparison, show that the groups differ in another way that could produce the result.
predictionHint: A third factor, such as better seed, coincides with the treatment.

stimulus: Mayor: Since the city launched its downtown ambassador program last year, thefts reported in the downtown district have fallen by 18 percent. Nothing else about downtown policing changed in that period, so the ambassador program deserves the credit, and it should now be expanded to every district in the city.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the mayor's argument?

choices.A: The ambassadors are not authorized to make arrests, and must call the police whenever they witness a crime.
choices.B: Over the past year, reported thefts rose slightly in several of the districts adjoining the downtown district.
choices.C: The program cost the city more than any other downtown initiative that it has undertaken in the past decade.
choices.D: Last year the city began excluding thefts of goods worth under fifty dollars from its reported-theft statistics.
choices.E: Several other cities have launched similar ambassador programs, and the results of those programs have varied.

explanations.A: True but irrelevant: ambassadors might deter theft without arresting anyone.
explanations.B: Half right: displacement would weaken the case for citywide expansion, but it does not show that the downtown decline is not real, and a small rise nearby may not offset it.
explanations.C: Out of scope: cost is not part of the mayor's case for credit.
explanations.D: Correct. If a change in what gets counted removed many thefts from the statistics, the 18 percent fall may be an artifact, undermining both the credit and the case for expansion.
explanations.E: Wrong force: varied results elsewhere do not show that the program failed here.

keyTakeaway: Before crediting a cause for a change in a statistic, check whether the measurement itself changed.
predictionHint: The measured decline may come from a change in how thefts are recorded.

stimulus: The Harlow Valley cheese cooperative prices its wheels of cheddar about 20 percent below the prices charged by its competitors. Nevertheless, the cooperative earns more profit on each wheel it sells than its competitors earn on theirs.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?

choices.A: The cooperative's cheddar is aged for the same length of time as the cheddar sold by its competitors.
choices.B: Most of the cooperative's customers buy several wheels of cheddar at a time rather than a single wheel.
choices.C: Consumers regard the cooperative's cheddar as being of high quality in comparison with other cheddars.
choices.D: The cooperative sells somewhat more wheels each year than most of its competitors do.
choices.E: The cooperative's per-wheel production cost is lower than its competitors' by more than the price gap.

explanations.A: Out of scope: equal aging gives no reason why profit per wheel should be higher.
explanations.B: Out of scope: multiple purchases bear on total sales, not on profit per wheel.
explanations.C: Wrong force: quality might sustain demand, but it does not explain higher profit at a lower price.
explanations.D: True but irrelevant: selling more wheels affects total profit, not profit on each wheel.
explanations.E: Correct. Profit per wheel is price minus cost; if costs are lower by more than the price gap, profit per wheel can be higher despite the lower price.

keyTakeaway: Resolve a profit paradox by finding what changes the other side of price minus cost.
predictionHint: Costs per wheel must be much lower than the competitors'.

stimulus: At the Tell Marun excavation, the grain-storage pits from the settlement's later period are much smaller than those from its earlier period. Yet archaeological estimates indicate that the later settlement had more inhabitants, and that its harvests were no smaller than those of the earlier period.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the difference in pit size described above?

choices.A: In the later period most grain was kept in above-ground granaries, with pits used only for seed grain.
choices.B: The pits from the earlier period were lined with clay, which helped to preserve them over the centuries.
choices.C: The population estimates for the later period are based on the number of house foundations found.
choices.D: Some of the pits from the earlier period were never used to store grain at all.
choices.E: Rainfall in the region was lower during the later period than during the earlier period of settlement.

explanations.A: Correct. If most grain was stored elsewhere, small pits are compatible with a larger population and unchanged harvests.
explanations.B: Out of scope: preservation of the pits does not explain their original size and could even suggest later pits were once larger.
explanations.C: True but irrelevant: how population was estimated does not explain why the pits are smaller.
explanations.D: Wrong force: unused earlier pits would not change the fact that the later ones are smaller.
explanations.E: Opposite: lower rainfall would reduce harvests, deepening the puzzle rather than resolving it.

keyTakeaway: To explain a discrepancy, show how both facts can hold by introducing a hidden difference.
predictionHint: Grain was stored somewhere other than the pits in the later period.

stimulus: Council member: The Fenwick farmers' market should be moved from its present side-street location to the town square. Foot traffic in the square is far heavier than on the side street, and vendors generally sell more where foot traffic is heavier. Vendors will therefore sell more in the square.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the council member's argument?

choices.A: The town square has more open space than the side street, which would allow for a larger number of stalls.
choices.B: Vendors at farmers' markets held in squares in other towns tend to charge higher prices than vendors elsewhere.
choices.C: Most of the people who pass through the square are the kind of shoppers who buy fresh produce and baked goods.
choices.D: Foot traffic in the square is heaviest on weekends, when the market is already open.
choices.E: Several vendors at the present market have said that they prefer the side street.

explanations.A: Out of scope: room for more stalls does not show that each vendor would sell more, and could even mean more competition.
explanations.B: Out of scope: higher prices elsewhere say nothing about how many goods Fenwick's vendors would sell.
explanations.C: Correct. It supports the link between more foot traffic and more sales by showing that the added passers-by are likely buyers of the vendors' goods.
explanations.D: Half right: it shows overlap with market hours but not that the extra people would buy; it is weaker than the correct answer.
explanations.E: Opposite: vendor preferences for the present location mildly weaken the case.

keyTakeaway: To strengthen a more-traffic-means-more-sales argument, show the added traffic is made of likely buyers.
predictionHint: The extra foot traffic would consist of people who buy what vendors sell.

stimulus: Historian: Guild ledgers show that raw-wool exports from the port of Calder fell sharply in the 1380s. Some scholars blame a plague that struck the region, but plague deaths among weavers would also have cut Calder's cloth exports, and the ledgers show that cloth exports from Calder actually rose in that decade. The fall in wool exports therefore reflects a shift by Calder's merchants toward turning the wool into cloth locally instead of shipping it raw.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the historian's argument?

choices.A: Many of the weavers who worked in Calder during the 1380s died of the plague that struck the region.
choices.B: Raw-wool exports from other ports in the region also fell during the 1380s.
choices.C: The clerks who kept the guild ledgers were paid according to the volume of goods that they recorded each year.
choices.D: The wool used by Calder's own cloth workshops in the 1380s rose by about as much as raw-wool exports fell.
choices.E: Cloth made in Calder in the 1380s was generally of higher quality than the cloth that had been made there earlier.

explanations.A: Opposite: weaver deaths support the scholars' plague explanation and leave the rising cloth exports harder to explain.
explanations.B: Opposite: a region-wide fall suggests a common cause such as the plague rather than a Calder-specific shift.
explanations.C: Out of scope: a payment scheme for clerks gives no reason to think the ledgers are wrong or the shift occurred.
explanations.D: Correct. It shows that the wool that stopped leaving as raw wool went into local cloth-making, directly supporting the claimed shift.
explanations.E: True but irrelevant: better quality does not show that more of the wool was turned into cloth rather than lost to plague.

keyTakeaway: After an argument rules out a rival cause, the best strengthener shows the proposed cause accounts for the quantity at issue.
predictionHint: Show the missing wool went into local cloth production.

stimulus: County executive: The county should not lease its fairgrounds to whichever bidder offers the highest price. The fairgrounds are a public asset that residents have used for generations.
stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the county executive's reasoning?

choices.A: A public asset should never be leased to a private party under any circumstances, whatever the price.
choices.B: A public asset long used by residents should not be leased on price alone.
choices.C: Residents should be consulted before any public asset that they have used is leased to a private party.
choices.D: Preserving a community's history is more important than raising revenue for the local government.
choices.E: A public asset that residents have used for generations should be preserved unchanged for future generations.

explanations.A: Extreme: the executive objects only to leasing to the highest bidder, not to leasing at all.
explanations.B: Correct. It links the premise (long-used public asset) to the conclusion (do not lease to the highest bidder) without going further.
explanations.C: Out of scope: consultation is not at issue, and consulting residents would not prevent a lease to the highest bidder.
explanations.D: Shell game: it invokes history and revenue, but the premise is about residents' use and the conclusion is about the way a lease is awarded.
explanations.E: Extreme: preserving the asset unchanged would bar any lease, going far beyond the conclusion.

keyTakeaway: A justifying principle should connect the premise's category to the conclusion's action and no further.
predictionHint: Long-used public assets should not be leased on price alone.

stimulus: Mayor: The council acted improperly in hiring Ms. Okoro to evaluate the water department. Several years ago, Ms. Okoro was paid for consulting work by a company that regularly bids on the department's contracts.
stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the mayor's reasoning?

choices.A: A person hired to evaluate an agency should be required to disclose any past financial dealings with companies connected to the agency.
choices.B: It is improper to hire an outside evaluator for an agency whose own employees are capable of evaluating it.
choices.C: It is improper to hire to evaluate an agency anyone who has any financial tie to the agency itself.
choices.D: It is improper to hire to evaluate an agency anyone who is currently being paid by a company that bids on the agency's contracts.
choices.E: It is improper to hire to evaluate an agency anyone who has at any time been paid by a company that bids on the agency's contracts.

explanations.A: Wrong force: a duty to disclose does not make the hiring improper, which is the mayor's conclusion.
explanations.B: Out of scope: Ms. Okoro's hiring is attacked on the basis of her past payment, not on whether the staff could have done the job.
explanations.C: Shell game: the mayor cites a tie to a company that bids on contracts, not a tie to the department itself.
explanations.D: Near miss: the premise concerns payment 'several years ago,' so Ms. Okoro is not shown to be 'currently' paid; this principle never applies to her.
explanations.E: Correct. 'At any time' covers a payment made several years ago by a company that bids on the department's contracts, so the principle applies and yields the conclusion.

keyTakeaway: A principle justifies a conclusion only if its stated conditions are actually met by the facts given, including time frame and relationship.
predictionHint: Anyone who has ever been paid by a bidding company is an improper evaluator.

stimulus: Farm bureau officer: Dunmore Farm cannot qualify for this year's organic subsidy, because the county has not inspected Dunmore Farm this year.
stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: Every farm that the county has inspected this year qualifies for the organic subsidy that is offered.
choices.B: The county will inspect Dunmore Farm early next year.
choices.C: Most farms that qualify for the subsidy were inspected by the county at some point this year.
choices.D: Only farms inspected by the county this year can qualify for the organic subsidy.
choices.E: Farms that the county has not inspected are poorly managed.

explanations.A: Reversal: this says inspection suffices for qualifying, but the argument needs inspection to be required.
explanations.B: Out of scope: next year's inspection says nothing about this year's subsidy.
explanations.C: Wrong force: 'most' leaves room for qualifying farms that were not inspected, which could include Dunmore.
explanations.D: Correct. If qualifying requires a county inspection this year, then lacking one rules Dunmore out.
explanations.E: Out of scope: management quality is not tied to the subsidy's requirements.

keyTakeaway: To conclude that something fails to qualify, assume the missing feature is required for qualifying.
predictionHint: Qualifying requires a county inspection this year.

stimulus: Council clerk: Every council member who read the full cost estimate voted for the amendment to the transit ordinance. Therefore, at least one council member who voted for the amendment voted against the ordinance itself.
stem: The clerk's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: At least one council member who read the full cost estimate voted against the ordinance.
choices.B: At least one council member who read the full cost estimate did not vote for the ordinance.
choices.C: At least one council member who voted for the amendment did not read the full cost estimate.
choices.D: No council member who voted for the ordinance read the full cost estimate.
choices.E: Every council member who voted against the ordinance read the full cost estimate.

explanations.A: Correct. A member who read the estimate and voted against the ordinance must, by the premise, have voted for the amendment, giving exactly the conclusion.
explanations.B: Near miss: a member who 'did not vote for' the ordinance may have abstained rather than voted against it, so the conclusion about voting 'against' does not follow.
explanations.C: Reversal: members who voted for the amendment without reading the estimate are not covered by the premise and tell us nothing about the ordinance vote.
explanations.D: Necessary v sufficient: even if no ordinance supporter read the estimate, no one is shown to have voted against the ordinance.
explanations.E: Reversal: it says all opponents read the estimate, but it does not guarantee that there were any opponents.

keyTakeaway: Check that the assumed claim guarantees both the existence of the group and the exact property named in the conclusion.
predictionHint: Some reader of the estimate voted against the ordinance, not merely failed to vote for it.

stimulus: Some scholars claim that the Lindqvist diaries are a hoax because the handwriting varies widely from one volume to the next. But handwriting commonly changes over the decades of a lifetime, especially as a writer ages and writes under different conditions. Hence the variation in the handwriting gives no reason to suspect that the diaries are a hoax.
stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.A: The Lindqvist diaries are not a hoax.
choices.B: The variation in the diaries' handwriting gives no reason to suspect a hoax.
choices.C: Handwriting commonly changes over the decades of a person's lifetime, especially as the writer ages.
choices.D: Some scholars claim that the Lindqvist diaries are a hoax because their handwriting varies widely.
choices.E: A writer's handwriting changes as the writer ages and writes under different conditions over the years.

explanations.A: Extreme: the argument removes one reason for suspecting a hoax; it does not claim the diaries are authentic.
explanations.B: Correct. Signaled by 'Hence,' this is what the other statements support.
explanations.C: Premise: it is offered as the reason that variation is unremarkable.
explanations.D: Wrong part: this is the view the author argues against.
explanations.E: Premise: it elaborates why handwriting changes and supports the conclusion.

keyTakeaway: A conclusion indicator such as 'hence' marks the claim the rest of the passage supports; do not overreach beyond it.
predictionHint: The handwriting variation is no reason to suspect a hoax.

stimulus: Some residents say the city's new composting mandate is unfair to apartment dwellers. But buildings of more than twenty units are exempt from the mandate, and smaller buildings receive shared compost bins at no charge. Since the mandate imposes no special burden on apartment dwellers, it cannot be unfair to them.
stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.A: Some residents say that the new composting mandate is unfair to apartment dwellers.
choices.B: Buildings of more than twenty units are exempt from the composting mandate.
choices.C: The composting mandate is not unfair to apartment dwellers.
choices.D: Smaller apartment buildings receive shared compost bins at no charge.
choices.E: The composting mandate imposes no special burden on apartment dwellers.

explanations.A: Wrong part: this is the objection the author answers.
explanations.B: Premise: one of the facts offered to show there is no special burden.
explanations.C: Correct. The final clause, 'it cannot be unfair to them,' is supported by the claim of no special burden, which in turn rests on the exemption and the free bins.
explanations.D: Premise: the second fact offered to show there is no special burden.
explanations.E: Half right: this is an intermediate conclusion that itself supports the final claim about fairness.

keyTakeaway: Separate intermediate conclusions from the main conclusion by asking which claim is not used to support any other.
predictionHint: Facts show no special burden, so the mandate is not unfair.

stimulus: Many residents believe that the Ridgeway bridge must be demolished because it is old. But age alone does not make a bridge unsafe. The engineering inspection found no structural defects in the Ridgeway bridge. Therefore, the bridge need not be demolished.
stem: The claim that age alone does not make a bridge unsafe plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.A: It is the main conclusion of the argument, which the remaining statements are offered to support.
choices.B: It is an intermediate conclusion that is supported by the findings of the engineering inspection.
choices.C: It is a position that the argument as a whole is designed to refute by appeal to evidence.
choices.D: It is an example offered to illustrate a generalization about the safety of old bridges.
choices.E: It is a premise that, together with the inspection finding, supports the main conclusion.

explanations.A: Wrong part: the main conclusion is the final sentence, signaled by 'Therefore.'
explanations.B: Wrong part: the claim is not derived from the inspection; it is stated independently and the inspection is a separate premise.
explanations.C: Opposite: the argument endorses the claim and uses it against the residents' belief.
explanations.D: Shell game: the claim is itself a general statement, not an example of one.
explanations.E: Correct. It answers the residents' reason for demolition, and with the inspection finding it supports the conclusion.

keyTakeaway: To find a claim's role, ask what it supports and what, if anything, supports it.
predictionHint: A premise, working with the inspection result, supporting the final conclusion.

stimulus: Every orchardist in the Eastvale cooperative grows heirloom varieties. Some growers of heirloom varieties sell at the Saturday market. So some orchardists in the Eastvale cooperative sell at the Saturday market.
stem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.A: Every clerk in the records office is a notary. Some clerks in the records office speak Spanish. So some notaries speak Spanish.
choices.B: Some of the manuscripts in the library are forgeries. Every forgery has been catalogued by the curator. So some manuscripts in the library have been catalogued by the curator.
choices.C: Every bridge in the district is inspected annually. Some roads in the district are not inspected annually. So some roads in the district are not bridges.
choices.D: Every tax assessor in the county holds a state license. Some license holders work for the school board. So some tax assessors in the county work for the school board.
choices.E: No member of the zoning panel owns land in the flood zone. Some owners of land in the flood zone live downtown. So some people who live downtown are not members of the zoning panel.

explanations.A: Not flawed: the notaries who speak Spanish are the clerks themselves, so the conclusion follows.
explanations.B: Not flawed: the forgeries among the manuscripts are catalogued, so the conclusion follows.
explanations.C: Not flawed: roads that are not inspected annually cannot be bridges, which are all inspected, so the conclusion follows.
explanations.D: Correct. All A are B; some B are C; so some A are C. The license holders who work for the school board may all be outside the group of assessors, exactly as in the original.
explanations.E: Not flawed: the downtown owners in the flood zone cannot be panel members, so the conclusion follows.

keyTakeaway: To match a quantifier flaw, translate each argument into letters and compare the structure, not the topic.
predictionHint: All A are B, some B are C, so some A are C: the overlap may lie outside A.

stimulus: Archaeologist: The collapse of the Orrin settlement must have been caused by either drought or invasion. There is no sign of burning or weapons at the site, so invasion is ruled out. Therefore, drought caused the collapse.
stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.A: The harbor board will approve the dredging only if funding is secured. Funding has been secured. So the board will approve the dredging.
choices.B: The missing ledger was either mislaid by the clerk or taken by a visitor. The desk logs show that the clerk never had the ledger in her keeping. So a visitor must have taken it.
choices.C: If the creek floods, the lower field is ruined. The creek did not flood this spring. So the lower field was not ruined.
choices.D: Wheat farmers in the north who adopted the new seed saw gains. The southern farmers resemble the northern ones in soil and climate. So southern farmers who adopt it will see gains.
choices.E: Every dairy in the county is inspected each year. The Hallam dairy is in the county. So the Hallam dairy is inspected each year.

explanations.A: Affirming the antecedent of a stated requirement: it reasons from a necessary condition to the result, not by eliminating an alternative.
explanations.B: Correct. Two possibilities are given, one is ruled out by evidence, and the other is concluded.
explanations.C: Reasons from a conditional by denying its antecedent; it does not eliminate alternatives.
explanations.D: Argument by analogy between northern and southern farmers; no alternatives are eliminated.
explanations.E: Applies a general rule to a particular case; again no elimination.

keyTakeaway: Describe the method abstractly first (two options, one eliminated) and then match the structure.
predictionHint: Either X or Y; not X; therefore Y.

stimulus:
Reyes: The Eastgate bridge is a local landmark, and landmarks deserve preservation even at a premium. So the city should repair the bridge rather than replace it.
Imani: I agree that landmark status counts for something. But repairing the bridge would cost twice as much as replacing it, and the city cannot justify that premium. The bridge should be replaced.
stem: Reyes and Imani disagree over whether

choices.A: the Eastgate bridge is in fact a local landmark that deserves some measure of special regard
choices.B: repairing the Eastgate bridge would cost the city more money than replacing it would
choices.C: the bridge's landmark status justifies paying more to repair it than to replace it
choices.D: landmark status is a consideration that counts for something in deciding what to do about a bridge
choices.E: the city's budget for bridge work is limited enough to constrain the options that it can choose

explanations.A: Both treat the bridge as a landmark: Reyes asserts it and Imani agrees that landmark status counts.
explanations.B: Reyes speaks of preservation 'at a premium,' so Reyes does not dispute that repair costs more.
explanations.C: Correct. Reyes holds that landmark status justifies the extra cost of repair; Imani holds that it does not.
explanations.D: Imani explicitly grants that landmark status counts for something, and Reyes plainly agrees.
explanations.E: Reyes never addresses the size of the budget, so there is no evidence of disagreement.

keyTakeaway: A point at issue must be something one speaker affirms and the other rejects; conceded points do not qualify.
predictionHint: Does landmark status justify the premium cost of repair?

stimulus: At the Millbrook harvest festival, every vendor who sells preserves also sells baked goods, and no vendor who sells baked goods accepts only cash. Some vendors who sell dairy products accept only cash.
stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.A: Some vendors who sell dairy products also sell baked goods.
choices.B: Every vendor who sells baked goods also sells preserves.
choices.C: No vendor who sells dairy products sells baked goods.
choices.D: Some vendors who sell preserves accept only cash.
choices.E: Some vendors who sell dairy products do not sell preserves.

explanations.A: Unsupported: the only dairy vendors mentioned accept only cash and so cannot sell baked goods; nothing shows any dairy vendor does.
explanations.B: Reversal: preserves imply baked goods, not the other way around.
explanations.C: Extreme: only some dairy vendors are known to accept only cash; others may sell baked goods.
explanations.D: Opposite: preserve sellers sell baked goods, and baked-goods sellers do not accept only cash.
explanations.E: Correct. Dairy vendors who accept only cash cannot sell baked goods, and therefore cannot sell preserves, so some dairy vendors do not sell preserves.

keyTakeaway: Chain the conditionals and their contrapositives, then check each answer for reversals and overstatements.
predictionHint: Cash-only vendors sell no baked goods and hence no preserves.

stimulus: The founding documents of Harrowgate were destroyed in a fire, so historians must rely on accounts of its founding written generations later. But those later accounts were written by people with a stake in the town's reputation, and such writers tend to flatter the town they write about. Therefore, ____.
stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?

choices.A: the destroyed founding documents must themselves have contained flattering claims about the town's origins
choices.B: no reliable account of how Harrowgate was founded can ever be assembled
choices.C: the fire that destroyed the founding documents was probably set deliberately
choices.D: historians should be cautious about the later accounts' favorable claims about the founding
choices.E: the later accounts of the town's founding are inaccurate in every detail that they happen to mention

explanations.A: Out of scope: the argument says nothing about what the destroyed documents contained.
explanations.B: Extreme: caution about flattery does not make reliable reconstruction impossible, since other evidence might exist.
explanations.C: Out of scope: the cause of the fire plays no role.
explanations.D: Correct. Reliance on sources that tend to flatter calls for caution about their favorable claims.
explanations.E: Extreme: a tendency to flatter does not make every detail inaccurate.

keyTakeaway: The completion should follow from the stated premises at their stated strength.
predictionHint: Be cautious about the flattering claims in the later accounts.

stimulus: Historian: Dunn argues that the horse collar was the sole cause of medieval Europe's population growth, noting that populations rose in every region soon after its adoption. But populations also rose in every region soon after the adoption of the heavy plow, and soon after the spread of the watermill. By Dunn's reasoning, each of these would be the sole cause, which is absurd. So Dunn's reasoning is unsound.
stem: The historian's argument proceeds by

choices.A: showing that the reasoning would equally support rival conclusions that cannot all be true
choices.B: undermining Dunn's conclusion by showing that the evidence cited in support of it is inaccurate
choices.C: rejecting Dunn's conclusion on the grounds that Dunn lacks the qualifications needed to draw it
choices.D: citing a counterexample to a universal generalization that Dunn states as part of his argument
choices.E: deriving a contradiction between Dunn's conclusion and one of Dunn's own stated premises

explanations.A: Correct. The historian applies Dunn's pattern to the plow and the watermill, yielding several 'sole causes,' which cannot all be true.
explanations.B: Opposite: the historian accepts Dunn's data (populations did rise) and attacks the inference instead.
explanations.C: Wrong part: no personal attack on Dunn's qualifications is made.
explanations.D: Shell game: no universal generalization is stated by Dunn, and the historian offers parallel cases, not a counterexample.
explanations.E: Wrong part: no premise of Dunn's contradicts his conclusion; the problem arises when the reasoning is applied elsewhere.

keyTakeaway: A reductio on a pattern of reasoning applies the pattern to parallel cases and shows an unacceptable result.
predictionHint: Same reasoning would crown the plow and watermill too, which cannot all be the sole cause.

stimulus:
Warden: The county seed bank is not worth funding, since the worth of such a bank depends on whether farmers plant its varieties, and no local farmer currently plants any of them.
Clerk: I grant that no local farmer currently plants any of them. But a seed bank's worth also lies in its protection against future blights, and ours holds the only surviving samples of several varieties. So it is worth funding.
stem: The warden and the clerk are committed to agreeing about which one of the following?

choices.A: No local farmer currently plants any variety held in the county seed bank.
choices.B: Local farmers have no interest in planting the varieties that are held in the county seed bank.
choices.C: A seed bank is valuable only if it protects against future blights of the crops it holds.
choices.D: The county seed bank holds the only surviving samples of several of the varieties it stores.
choices.E: Funding for the county seed bank should be continued in the coming budget year.

explanations.A: Correct. The warden asserts it and the clerk explicitly grants it.
explanations.B: Near miss: the clerk grants only that no farmer currently plants the varieties, not that farmers lack interest in them.
explanations.C: Wrong part: the clerk says blight protection is part of a bank's worth; neither speaker says it is the only source of value.
explanations.D: Out of scope: only the clerk asserts this; the warden never addresses it.
explanations.E: Opposite: the speakers reach opposite conclusions about funding.

keyTakeaway: The point of agreement is often a fact one speaker asserts and the other concedes while still reaching a different conclusion.
predictionHint: The clerk concedes the warden's factual premise.
